nameStory: Staurastrum anchora gets its species name from the Latin word 'anchora,' meaning anchor, because its distinctive spiny projections resemble the arms of a ship's anchor. The genus name Staurastrum comes from Greek words meaning 'cross' and 'star,' referring to the star-like or cross-shaped appearance these tiny algae display when viewed under a microscope.
description: Staurastrum anchora is a microscopic green alga that lives in freshwater environments like ponds and lakes. This single-celled organism is so tiny you'd need a microscope to see it properly - it's only about 30-50 micrometers across (much smaller than the width of a human hair). It has a distinctive star-like shape with spiny projections that radiate outward from its center, giving it an ornate, almost crystalline appearance. Like other green algae, it makes its own food through photosynthesis and plays an important role in aquatic food webs.

idTips.label: Anchor-like projections
idTips.description: The cell has distinctive spiny arms that branch and curve like an anchor, with the projections typically showing bifurcated (two-pronged) tips that are the key identifying feature

idTips.label: Star-shaped symmetry
idTips.description: The overall form shows radial symmetry with projections extending outward from a central body, creating a star or cross-like pattern when viewed from above

idTips.label: Green coloration
idTips.description: The cell appears bright green under the microscope due to chlorophyll, though this may vary depending on lighting and staining techniques used

idTips.label: Cell wall ornamentation
idTips.description: The cell surface may show fine granular texturing or small bumps, giving it a slightly rough appearance rather than being perfectly smooth

idTips.label: Size range
idTips.description: Measures roughly 30-50 micrometers across including the projections, making it visible only under higher microscope magnifications

habitat: This microscopic alga lives in clean, freshwater environments including ponds, small lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. It prefers slightly acidic to neutral water and is often found in areas with good light penetration where it can photosynthesize effectively. You're most likely to encounter it in samples from pristine mountain ponds or clean suburban water bodies rather than polluted urban waterways.

seasonality.spring: Peak growing season begins as water temperatures warm and daylight increases, making this the best time to find active, healthy specimens in water samples.
seasonality.summer: Most abundant during warm summer months when conditions are optimal for photosynthesis and reproduction, though populations may decline during very hot, dry periods.
seasonality.fall: Still present but populations may begin to decline as temperatures cool and daylight decreases, though specimens can still be found in protected water bodies.
seasonality.winter: Survives in dormant stages or reduced numbers under ice cover, making it much less common in winter water samples from frozen ponds and lakes.

funFact: Despite being a single-celled organism smaller than a speck of dust, Staurastrum anchora is essentially a living jewel - each individual cell is like a tiny green crystal sculpture that builds itself, and some species in this genus are so beautiful that Victorian microscopists collected and arranged them into artistic displays for entertainment!
confusionNotes: Can be confused with other spiny Staurastrum species, but the anchor-like bifurcated (two-pronged) tips of the projections are diagnostic - think of it as 'tiny anchors' versus the straight spines or different branching patterns of its relatives.
contextualKnowledge: With only one recorded observation in New England, this species appears to be quite rare in our region, so finding it would be an exciting discovery for any freshwater microscopist. The Staurastrum genus contains some of the most ornate and beautiful microscopic organisms on Earth, often called 'living jewels' by those who study them.
compareHints: Staurastrum anchora differs from its relatives by its distinctive anchor-shaped projections with bifurcated tips, while species like S. longispinum has long straight spines and S. tetracerum has four-sided projections. The anchor-like branching pattern is unique within the genus and makes identification relatively straightforward once you know what to look for under the microscope.
